title: Episode 24: GitHub Discussions
description: Forum-style conversations, Q&A, polls, and navigation with screen readers.
concepts: What Discussions are: threaded community conversations on a repo
How Discussions differ from Issues: Q&A versus task tracking
Discussion categories: General, Q&A, Ideas, Show and Tell, Announcements
Replying and marking answers in Q&A discussions
Navigating discussions with a screen reader: headings and landmarks
Converting a discussion to an issue when action is needed
When to use Discussions versus Issues versus PRs
transcriptText:
[ALEX]
Welcome back. Today we’re exploring two GitHub features that support community learning and lightweight sharing: Discussions and Gists. These come up a lot once you move beyond just cloning a repository or opening your first issue.

[JAMIE]
And they’re easy to confuse with other GitHub features, right? Like, a learner might think, "If I have a question, should that be an issue?" Or, "If I want to share a code snippet, do I need a whole repository?"

[ALEX]
Exactly. And for blind and low-vision learners, there’s also a navigation question: where are these features, how do they behave with screen readers, and what should you expect from the layout? We’ll walk through all of that.

[PAUSE]
[ALEX]
Let’s start with Discussions. GitHub Discussions is a built-in forum space for repositories and organizations. It’s meant for open-ended conversation: questions, ideas, announcements, polls, and community knowledge sharing.

[JAMIE]
So this is different from issues and pull requests because it’s less about tracked work and more about conversation.

[ALEX]
That’s the key distinction. Issues imply actionable work. A bug report, a feature request, something that might get assigned, labeled, closed, or linked to ongoing development. Discussions are for talking things through without automatically signaling, "A maintainer needs to take action on this right now."

[JAMIE]
That seems important for maintainers too.

[ALEX]
Very important. If you post a support question as an issue, it can create noise. It inflates issue counts and suggests workflow urgency. The same question in Discussions is often a much better fit because it invites conversation without pretending it’s a tracked defect or task.

[JAMIE]
Can you give us the practical split?

[ALEX]
Sure. Use an issue when you found a bug, want a specific feature, need progress tracking, or expect an outcome like fixed, closed, or won’t fix. Use a discussion when you have a question, want community input, want to brainstorm before filing a feature request, or you’re opening something that may not have a single correct answer.

[JAMIE]
So if I’m wondering how a workflow works, or asking the community how they use a tool, that’s usually a discussion.

[ALEX]
Yes. And many repositories organize Discussions into categories. Common ones include Q and A for support questions, Ideas for brainstorming, Announcements for maintainer updates, General for broad conversation, and Show and Tell for sharing what you built.

[PAUSE]
[ALEX]
There’s also some workshop support guidance connected to this. If you’re a workshop alum looking for ongoing help, the recommended flow is to use the support hub. Start by reading pinned Start Here resources in Discussions. Search existing discussions before opening a new support thread. And if you hit a setup blocker or an accessibility blocker, use the support repository’s issue templates so maintainers can help more efficiently.

[JAMIE]
That’s a nice example of choosing the right channel. Community conversation in Discussions, trackable blockers in Issues.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]
[JAMIE]
How do learners actually get to Discussions?

[ALEX]
There are two common paths. First, from a repository. Navigate to the repo and look in the main navigation bar, where you usually find Code, Issues, Pull Requests, Actions, and similar tabs. If Discussions is enabled, there will be a Discussions tab there.

[JAMIE]
And if I’m using a screen reader?

[ALEX]
You may be able to press T to move among tab items, or K to navigate links and find the Discussions link. Then press Enter to open it.

[JAMIE]
What if the tab isn’t there?

[ALEX]
That does not necessarily mean you’re lost. Discussions is an opt-in feature. Maintainers have to enable it in repository settings, so not every repository uses it.

[JAMIE]
And the second path?

[ALEX]
From an organization. Larger organizations can have organization-level Discussions that are separate from any individual repository. So you go to the organization page, look for a Discussions tab there, and those conversations are community-wide rather than tied to one repo.

[PAUSE]
[ALEX]
Once you’re inside Discussions, categories matter a lot. The home page is organized by category, and each category acts like its own section.

[JAMIE]
So the layout isn’t just one big flat list.

[ALEX]
Right. For keyboard and screen reader users, category headings are useful landmarks. You may use heading navigation or a key like 3, depending on your setup, to jump among category headings. Then K may help move through discussion titles within a category, and Enter opens the discussion you want.

[JAMIE]
And for low-vision users, there’s a sidebar too, right?

[ALEX]
Yes. Depending on viewport width, the side panel may appear on the left or the right. It typically shows all categories with item counts, a pinned or announcements area near the top, most active discussions, and sometimes tags if the repository uses them.

[JAMIE]
That’s helpful because zoom level can really change where that panel appears.

[ALEX]
Exactly. It’s worth saying out loud: if something seems missing, try scanning the opposite side of the page or adjusting your viewport. The interface can reflow.

[PAUSE]
[JAMIE]
Okay, let’s say I want to start a new discussion.

[ALEX]
From the Discussions tab, activate the New discussion button. Then choose a category. That part matters because the category affects what kind of conversation you’re creating and sometimes what options appear.

[JAMIE]
What comes next?

[ALEX]
You fill in a title and body. The title should be clear and searchable. For example, "How do I use the daily-briefing agent?" is much better than just "Help." In the Q and A category, phrase the title as a question. That improves clarity and makes search results more meaningful.

[JAMIE]
And the body uses Markdown, like issues do?

[ALEX]
Yes. Same general editor behavior as issue comments. Then activate Start discussion to post.

[JAMIE]
Can you give the screen reader path step by step?

[ALEX]
Yes. Tab to the New discussion button and press Enter. In the category list, use arrow keys to select a category and press Enter. Then move to the title field and type your title. Tab to the body editor, enter Focus Mode to type or paste your content, then tab to Start discussion and press Enter. In many contexts, Ctrl+Enter can submit as well.

[JAMIE]
And before posting, search first.

[ALEX]
Absolutely. Search existing discussions before opening a new one. You can use the search bar on the Discussions page or GitHub’s search syntax with something like repo:owner slash name in:discussions.

[PAUSE]
[ALEX]
A few accessibility and usability reminders here. For screen reader users, the category selector usually comes first, then the title field, then the body editor. For low-vision users, the category choices may appear as a list or grid with names and descriptions, and the form usually becomes a stacked single-column layout at higher zoom. After posting, a green success banner may appear near the top, so if you don’t hear or see confirmation where you are, scroll or navigate back upward.

[JAMIE]
And for sighted users, this will look a lot like opening a new issue.

[ALEX]
Very similar, yes.

[PAUSE]
[JAMIE]
Once a discussion exists, how do I read and participate in it?

[ALEX]
A discussion page is structured much like an issue page. You’ll usually find the original post at the top, replies in chronological order, and a reply editor at the bottom. In Q and A discussions, if an answer has been accepted, that answered reply may be pinned near the top and marked clearly.

[JAMIE]
What about navigation?

[ALEX]
Heading navigation is useful. You can jump between the original post heading and reply headings. Then arrow through content to read. Replies are often exposed as article elements, which is especially useful for screen reader users.

[JAMIE]
So if I’m using NVDA or JAWS, article navigation can help me move reply by reply.

[ALEX]
Exactly. In many cases, pressing A jumps among article elements, which often correspond to replies. That can make long threads much more manageable.

[JAMIE]
How do I reply?

[ALEX]
You can go to the main reply editor near the bottom of the page, enter Focus Mode, type your reply, and submit, often with Ctrl+Enter. The editor behaves like issue comments.

[JAMIE]
And if I want to respond to one specific comment?

[ALEX]
Use that comment’s Reply button. Tab to Reply under the specific comment, press Enter, and a nested text area opens beneath it. Then enter Focus Mode, type, and submit with Ctrl+Enter.

[JAMIE]
Nice. That helps keep conversation context clear.

[ALEX]
Exactly. And one etiquette point: instead of posting "+1," use the thumbs-up reaction or other reactions. Many maintainers look at upvotes to identify the most useful responses or the most requested ideas.

[PAUSE]
[JAMIE]
Now let’s talk about accepted answers, because that’s one of the most distinctive parts of Q and A discussions.

[ALEX]
Right. In the Q and A category, one answer can be marked as the accepted answer. That helps future readers get to the solution quickly.

[JAMIE]
Who can mark an answer?

[ALEX]
Typically the discussion author can do it, and repository maintainers may also have that ability depending on permissions. The basic process is to locate the correct reply and activate the control to mark it as the answer.

[JAMIE]
And what changes once it’s marked?

[ALEX]
You usually get a visible answered state, often a green Answered badge near the discussion title, and the accepted answer may be pinned toward the top above the rest of the reply timeline. That’s useful for everyone, and especially helpful when navigating with a screen reader because it reduces the amount of searching for the final resolution.

[JAMIE]
So if I asked the question, I should come back and mark the reply that solved it.

[ALEX]
Please do. It’s a kindness to the next learner.

[PAUSE]
[JAMIE]
Discussions can also include polls, right?

[ALEX]
Yes. Some communities use polls to gather quick input. A poll lets the author add a question and multiple answer options so people can vote.

[JAMIE]
What should learners know about creating a poll?

[ALEX]
First, polls depend on repository settings and category support, so they may not be available everywhere. When they are available, the creation flow usually includes fields for poll choices as part of the discussion form. You enter the discussion title and context, then add the poll options.

[JAMIE]
And voting?

[ALEX]
Readers choose an option and submit their vote. After voting, results are commonly displayed with percentages. For low-vision users, note that the interface may use color-filled bars to indicate proportion, so don’t rely on color alone; look or listen for percentage text when available.

[PAUSE]
[ALEX]
Let’s pause for a more focused screen reader navigation reference for Discussions.

[JAMIE]
Perfect. This is the kind of thing learners often want all in one place.

[ALEX]
On the Discussions list page, look for the Discussions tab in the repository or organization navigation. Use heading navigation to move among category sections. Use link or tab navigation to find discussion titles. The sidebar with category counts, pinned content, active discussions, and tags may be placed differently depending on screen width.

Inside an individual discussion, the main post is near the top, replies follow, and the editor is near the bottom. Replies are often article elements.

For NVDA users, article navigation can be especially handy for moving among replies. For JAWS users, the same article quick key often works as well. For VoiceOver users, rotor navigation by headings, links, or landmarks may be more practical depending on browser and verbosity settings.

[JAMIE]
So the exact key pattern can vary, but the underlying structure is still pretty navigable.

[ALEX]
That’s right. The big idea is to use headings for overall structure, articles for reply-by-reply movement where supported, and Focus Mode when entering text.

[PAUSE]
[JAMIE]
What about organization-level Discussions? We touched on them earlier, but let’s make the distinction explicit.

[ALEX]
Good idea. Repository-level Discussions belong to one project. Organization-level Discussions belong to the broader organization community. That means the conversation may be about shared practices, support across multiple repositories, community announcements, or organization-wide Q and A.

[JAMIE]
So if I’m in a large org with many repos, I should pay attention to whether I’m asking something repo-specific or community-wide.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Asking in the right place improves your chances of getting useful help.

[PAUSE]
[JAMIE]
There’s also a section here about accessibility agents and what’s different in Discussions. What should learners take from that?

[ALEX]
A few things. Discussions often feel less rigid than issues. That can be helpful, but it also means more conversational content to skim. Accessibility tools, screen readers, and AI assistants may need stronger prompting from you: ask for the accepted answer, ask for the highest-upvoted reply, ask whether a thread is Q and A or General, and ask for the category if that context matters.

[JAMIE]
So the challenge isn’t just navigation. It’s also interpretation.

[ALEX]
Exactly. In issues, the status may be obvious: open, closed, assigned. In Discussions, you may need to infer whether a question was answered, whether a thread is still active, or whether a maintainer announcement is just informational. For blind and low-vision users working with accessibility agents or AI summarizers, it helps to ask targeted questions like, "Is there an accepted answer?" "What category is this in?" or "Are there polls or upvoted replies I should know about?"

[PAUSE]
[ALEX]
Now let’s shift to Gists.

[JAMIE]
These are one of those GitHub features people hear about early, but often don’t quite understand.

[ALEX]
That’s true. A Gist is a lightweight way to share code snippets, notes, small examples, or short multi-file content on GitHub without creating a full repository in the usual sense.

[JAMIE]
So if Discussions are for community conversation, Gists are for shareable bits of content.

[ALEX]
Exactly. You can think of a Gist as a simple container for one or more files that you want to publish or share quickly.

[JAMIE]
And there are learning cues here too, right?

[ALEX]
Yes. For screen reader users, Gists are usually straightforward forms with file name and content editors, but it’s helpful to know where file controls are. For low-vision users, the page is often visually simpler than a full repository. For sighted users, it feels like a lightweight code-sharing interface rather than a project workspace.

[PAUSE]
[JAMIE]
So what exactly is a Gist?

[ALEX]
A Gist is a shareable collection of one or more files hosted by GitHub. It’s often used for quick code examples, Markdown notes, configuration snippets, reproducible examples, or reference text you want to link to.

[JAMIE]
Can a Gist be versioned?

[ALEX]
Yes. Gists do keep revision history. You can edit them, and GitHub tracks changes over time. They also support Git operations like cloning and forking.

[JAMIE]
That surprises some people.

[ALEX]
It does. Gists are lighter than repositories in presentation and purpose, but they still have real Git behavior behind them.

[PAUSE]
[JAMIE]
When should someone use a Gist instead of a repository?

[ALEX]
Use a Gist when the content is small, self-contained, and primarily meant for sharing rather than ongoing project collaboration. For example: a short code snippet for an answer, a one-page Markdown note, a sample config file, or a tiny reproducible example.

[JAMIE]
And a repository is better when the thing has structure, issues, branches, documentation, or a life as an actual project.

[ALEX]
Exactly. If you need project organization, multiple contributors, a README-driven home page, issue tracking, pull requests, or a longer-term development workflow, use a repository.

[JAMIE]
So a Gist is not just "a tiny repo," even though some Git features overlap.

[ALEX]
Right. The overlap is real, but the intended use is different.

[PAUSE]
[JAMIE]
Walk us through creating a Gist on the web.

[ALEX]
You go to the Gist creation interface on GitHub. Then you provide a file name, add content, and optionally a description for the Gist itself. You choose whether to create it as public or secret, then activate the create button.

[JAMIE]
What do public and secret mean here?

[ALEX]
Public Gists are discoverable and visible to others. Secret Gists are not shown in public listings, but anyone with the link can access them. Secret does not mean secure or private in a strong sense.

[JAMIE]
That distinction matters a lot.

[ALEX]
It does. Never put sensitive data in a Gist. Not passwords, tokens, private keys, personal confidential information, or anything you would regret if shared.

[PAUSE]
[JAMIE]
Can you describe the screen reader navigation for creating a Gist?

[ALEX]
Typically, you navigate to the description field if present, then to the first file name field, then to the editor for file contents. After that, you move to the create controls and choose either public or secret creation. As with other GitHub editors, entering Focus Mode in the code or text editor may be necessary depending on your setup.

[JAMIE]
And if I need more than one file?

[ALEX]
You can add multiple files to a Gist. There’s usually an Add file control. Each file gets its own file name field and content editor. That’s useful when your snippet makes sense only with a companion Markdown explanation, stylesheet, config file, or small supporting script.

[JAMIE]
So a Gist can be more than a single paste box.

[ALEX]
Definitely.

[PAUSE]
[ALEX]
A few practical creation reminders. Choose descriptive file names so syntax highlighting and interpretation work correctly. If you’re sharing notes, a Markdown file can be a good choice. If you’re sharing code, use an appropriate extension. And just like with discussions, write clear descriptions when you can—they make your content easier to revisit later.

[JAMIE]
That sounds obvious until you’re staring at ten unnamed snippets six weeks later.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]
[JAMIE]
What about editing a Gist?

[ALEX]
If you own the Gist, you can open it and use the Edit action. Then update the file contents, file names, description, or files themselves, and save the changes. GitHub keeps revision history, so edits become part of that record.

[JAMIE]
Can you embed a Gist elsewhere?

[ALEX]
Yes. Gists can often be embedded into web pages using the embed script GitHub provides. That makes them useful for blog posts, documentation pages, or demos where you want the code displayed from a maintained source.

[JAMIE]
And cloning?

[ALEX]
A Gist can be cloned with Git, just like a repository URL. That means you can pull it down locally, inspect it in VS Code, make changes, and push updates if it’s yours.

[JAMIE]
And forking?

[ALEX]
You can fork a Gist too. That’s useful if someone shared a snippet you want to adapt while preserving the original. Forking creates your own copy.

[PAUSE]
[JAMIE]
How do I find my Gists later?

[ALEX]
GitHub provides ways to access your own Gists from your account area and Gist pages. Once there, you can review your created Gists, starred items if supported in your workflow, and individual entries.

[JAMIE]
Any screen reader notes?

[ALEX]
Use heading and link navigation to move through the list. Listen for descriptions, file names, and metadata like whether the Gist is public or secret if that’s exposed in the interface. Because Gist listings are typically compact, consistent heading or link navigation works well.

[JAMIE]
And what about discovering other people’s public Gists?

[ALEX]
Public Gists can be browsed and discovered through GitHub’s Gist interfaces and shared links. But remember: public means public. Treat anything you publish there as openly accessible.

[PAUSE]
[JAMIE]
Can people comment on Gists?

[ALEX]
Yes. Gists support comments. To add a comment, open the Gist, move to the comment area, enter your text in the comment editor, and submit. The interaction is familiar if you’ve used issue or discussion comments.

[JAMIE]
So even a quick snippet can turn into a little conversation.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]
[JAMIE]
Let’s linger on security and privacy, because this is where people get into trouble.

[ALEX]
Agreed. Public Gists are openly visible and should be treated as fully public. Secret Gists are unlisted rather than truly private. Anyone with the link can access them, and links can be shared or leaked.

[JAMIE]
So secret is more like obscured, not protected.

[ALEX]
That’s the right mental model. And the biggest rule is simple: never put sensitive data in a Gist. No credentials, no secrets, no internal-only information you’re not prepared to expose.

[JAMIE]
That warning is worth repeating because people often use Gists for quick sharing and move too fast.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]
[JAMIE]
Can we give a few example use cases?

[ALEX]
Absolutely. One example is sharing screen reader configuration. If you wanted to share NVDA settings for GitHub web navigation, a Gist could hold a config file or a note describing recommended settings and shortcuts. That makes it easy to link in a discussion, workshop message, or support response.

[JAMIE]
Another one was a quick Markdown note.

[ALEX]
Yes. Imagine a "Workshop Day 1 Notes" Gist containing a Markdown file with setup reminders, command references, or links collected during training. That’s a perfect lightweight use case.

[JAMIE]
And a third is a code snippet for answering someone on Stack Overflow or in a GitHub discussion.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Instead of pasting a huge block inline, you can put the code in a Gist and link to it.

[PAUSE]
[JAMIE]
Can you give us a quick comparison between Gists and repositories?

[ALEX]
Sure. Gists are best for small, focused, easily shared files or snippets. Repositories are best for complete projects. Gists are lightweight and fast to create. Repositories support richer collaboration and project structure. Both can be versioned with Git, but repositories provide the fuller development workflow.

[JAMIE]
So if I’m unsure, I can ask: is this a shareable snippet, or is this a project?

[ALEX]
That’s a very good test.

[PAUSE]
[JAMIE]
And if I no longer need a Gist?

[ALEX]
You can delete it from the Gist’s controls if it belongs to you. As always, confirm carefully before deleting. If others rely on the link, removing the Gist may break references.

[PAUSE]
[JAMIE]
Before we wrap up, what are the big learning cards you want listeners to remember?

[ALEX]
For Discussions: the Discussions tab lives alongside the main repository tabs when enabled. Categories shape the kind of conversation. Q and A threads can have accepted answers. Replies often behave like article elements, so screen reader navigation can be efficient. Use reactions instead of "+1" comments. Search before posting.

For Gists: use them for snippets, notes, and small multi-file shares. They can be created on the web, edited later, cloned, forked, embedded, and commented on. Public is public. Secret is unlisted, not truly private. Never store sensitive data there.

[JAMIE]
And maybe one more theme connects both features: choose the lightest tool that fits your goal.

[ALEX]
Exactly. If you need community conversation, use Discussions rather than forcing everything into Issues. If you need to share a small piece of code or notes, use a Gist rather than creating a whole repository.

[JAMIE]
That makes GitHub feel less like one giant undifferentiated platform and more like a set of tools with distinct jobs.

[ALEX]
Well said. And the more clearly you choose the right space, the easier it becomes for maintainers, classmates, and future you to understand what you meant.

[PAUSE]
[ALEX]
For authoritative follow-up reading, GitHub Docs remains the main source for Discussions and Gists behavior, and GitHub’s changelog can help you catch interface changes over time.

[JAMIE]
And from an accessibility perspective, remember that layouts can shift, sidebars can move, accepted answers can be pinned, and editor focus behavior matters. Slow down, use structure, and ask your tools precise questions.

[ALEX]
Exactly. That’s it for today. Next time you’re deciding where a question belongs or how to share a useful snippet, you’ll know which GitHub feature fits the job.

# Appendix U: Discussions and Gists

> **Reference companion to:** [Chapter 08: Open Source Culture](08-open-source-culture.md) | Also relevant: [Chapter 10](10-notifications-and-day-1-close.md)
>
> **Authoritative source:** [GitHub Docs: About discussions](https://docs.github.com/en/discussions)

> This appendix consolidates two related community content features: GitHub Discussions (formerly Appendix G) and GitHub Gists (formerly Appendix F).

---

## GitHub Discussions

>
> **Listen to Episode 24:** [GitHub Discussions](https://lp.csedesigns.com/ggg/PODCASTS.html) - a conversational audio overview of this chapter. Listen before reading to preview the concepts, or after to reinforce what you learned.

## Forum-Style Conversations Beyond Issues and Pull Requests

> GitHub Discussions is a built-in community forum for repositories and organizations. It's where open-ended conversations live - questions, ideas, announcements, polls, and community Q&A - separate from the action-oriented world of issues and pull requests.

### Support Hub Onboarding (Recommended For Workshop Alumni)

For ongoing support after the workshop, use:

- Support hub home: [Community-Access/support](https://github.com/Community-Access/support)
- Q&A and community discussion: [Support Hub Discussions](https://github.com/Community-Access/support/discussions)
- Trackable support requests: [Support Hub Issues](https://github.com/Community-Access/support/issues)

Suggested first steps for students:

1. Read the pinned Start Here resources in Discussions.
2. Search existing discussions before opening a new support thread.
3. Use issue templates for setup blockers or accessibility blockers so maintainers can help faster.

### Learning Cards: GitHub Discussions

<details>
<summary>Screen reader users</summary>

- The Discussions tab is in the repository's main navigation bar alongside Code, Issues, and Pull Requests -- press `T` to navigate tab items or `K` to find the "Discussions" link
- Inside a discussion, replies are `article` elements -- in NVDA press `A` to jump between replies; in JAWS use `A` as well
- The reply editor uses the same behavior as issue comments -- enter Focus Mode to type, then press `Ctrl+Enter` to submit

</details>

<details>
<summary>Low vision users</summary>

- Discussion categories appear as a sidebar panel on the left or right depending on viewport width -- look for the category list with item counts
- Answered discussions in the Q&A category display a green "Answered" badge next to the title, with the accepted answer pinned to the top
- Polls show percentage bars next to each option after you vote -- the bars use color fill to indicate proportion

</details>

<details>
<summary>Sighted users</summary>

- Discussions are organized by category with colored labels -- the sidebar shows all categories and pinned items
- In Q&A threads, look for the green checkmark on the accepted answer pinned above the regular reply timeline
- Use the upvote button (thumbs up) on replies instead of posting "+1" comments -- maintainers often sort by upvotes

</details>

## Table of Contents

1. [Discussions vs. Issues: When to Use Which](#1-discussions-vs-issues-when-to-use-which)
2. [Navigating to Discussions](#2-navigating-to-discussions)
3. [Discussion Categories](#3-discussion-categories)
4. [Creating a Discussion](#4-creating-a-discussion)
5. [Participating in Discussions](#5-participating-in-discussions)
6. [Marking an Answer](#6-marking-an-answer)
7. [Polls](#7-polls)
8. [Screen Reader Navigation Reference](#8-screen-reader-navigation-reference)
9. [Organization-Level Discussions](#9-organization-level-discussions)
10. [Accessibility Agents: What's Different Here](#10-accessibility-agents-whats-different-here)

## 1. Discussions vs. Issues: When to Use Which

**Not every conversation belongs in an issue.** GitHub Discussions exists for the conversations that don't fit:

| Use Issues When | Use Discussions When |
| ---  | ---  |
| You found a bug | You have a question about how something works |
| You want to request a specific feature | You want to brainstorm ideas before filing a feature request |
| There is actionable work to be done | You want community input before deciding what work to do |
| You need to track progress (labels, assign, close) | You want to have an open conversation without resolving it |
| The answer is "fixed" or "won't fix" | The conversation might not have one right answer |

**The signal for maintainers:** A question in an issue is noisier - it implies something needs to be done. The same question in Discussions doesn't trigger workflow automation and doesn't inflate the issue count.

### Common Discussions categories you'll encounter

- **Q&A** - Support questions and answers (one answer can be marked correct)
- **Ideas** - Feature brainstorming before a formal feature request
- **Announcements** - Maintainer posts about releases, breaking changes, roadmaps
- **General** - Everything else
- **Show and Tell** - Community members showing what they built

## 2. Navigating to Discussions

### From a Repository

1. Navigate to the repository
2. There is a **Discussions** tab in the main navigation (alongside Code, Issues, Pull Requests, Actions, Projects)
3. Press `T` to navigate tab items, or `K` to navigate links and find "Discussions"
4. Press `Enter` to open

**If the tab is missing:** Discussions is an opt-in feature. The repository maintainer must enable it in Settings. Not all repositories use it.

### From an Organization

Large organizations can have organization-level Discussions separate from any individual repository:

1. Navigate to the organization page
2. Look for the Discussions tab at the organization level
3. These are community-wide conversations, not repo-specific

## 3. Discussion Categories

The Discussions home page is organized by category. Each category is a section with its own heading.

### Navigating categories

```text
3 → Jump to category headings
K → Navigate discussion titles within a category
Enter → Open a discussion
```

### The side panel (left or right depending on view width) shows

- All categories with item counts
- Pin/announcements section at top
- Most active discussions
- Tags (if the repo uses them)

## 4. Creating a Discussion

1. From the Discussions tab, activate **"New discussion"** button
2. Select a category (required - affects which fields appear)
3. Fill in:
   - **Title** - Clear and searchable. "How do I use the daily-briefing agent?" not "Help"
   - **Body** - Use Markdown. Same editor as issues
   - For **Q&A** category: phrase the title as a question
4. Activate **"Start discussion"**

### Screen reader path

```text
Tab to "New discussion" button → Enter
→ Category list: ↑/↓ to select category → Enter
→ Title field: type title
→ Tab to body: Focus Mode → type or paste content
→ Tab to "Start discussion" button → Enter
```

**Before posting a question:** Search existing discussions first. Use the search bar at the top of the Discussions page or GitHub's global search with `repo:owner/name in:discussions`.

### Learning Cards: Creating a Discussion

**Screen reader users:**

- Tab to the "New discussion" button from the Discussions tab, then press Enter -- the form loads with a category selector first; arrow through categories and press Enter to select
- The title field comes after the category selector -- type a clear, searchable title; for Q&A category, phrase it as a question so it reads naturally in search results
- The body editor is the same as the issue comment editor -- enter Focus Mode to type, use Markdown formatting, and press `Ctrl+Enter` to submit the discussion

**Low-vision users:**

- The category selector appears as a list or grid of labeled options -- each category has a name and description; zoom in to read the descriptions and pick the right one
- The title and body fields stack vertically in a single-column layout -- the form is the same width as the main content area, making it easy to scan at high zoom
- After creating a discussion, a green success banner appears at the top -- scroll up if you do not see confirmation at your current zoom position

**Sighted users:**

- Categories appear as clickable cards or a list when creating a new discussion -- choose Q&A for questions (allows marking an answer), Ideas for brainstorming, General for everything else
- The "New discussion" button is prominently placed at the top-right of the Discussions tab -- the form layout is nearly identical to the new issue form
- Search existing discussions before posting -- use the search bar at the top of the Discussions page to avoid duplicate questions

## 5. Participating in Discussions

### Reading a Discussion

A discussion page is structured similarly to an issue:

- The original post at the top
- Replies in chronological order
- An "Answered" reply pinned to the top (Q&A category only)
- A reply editor at the bottom

#### Navigation

```text
H → Jump between the original post heading and reply headings
3 → Navigate individual reply headings
↓ → Read through content
```

### Replying to a Discussion

1. Navigate to the bottom of the page (or use the "Reply" button on a specific comment)
2. The reply text area behaves identically to issue comments
3. Focus Mode → type your reply
4. `Ctrl+Enter` to submit

### Replying to a Specific Comment (Nested Reply)

Each comment has a **Reply** button below it:

```text
Tab to "Reply" button on the specific comment → Enter
→ Nested text area opens under that comment
→ Focus Mode → type → Ctrl+Enter
```

### Upvoting

Instead of leaving "+1" comments, use the thumbs-up reaction on the original post or replies. Many maintainers sort discussion responses by upvotes to prioritize most-needed answers.

## 6. Marking an Answer

In the **Q&A** category, one reply can be marked as the accepted answer. This is similar to Stack Overflow's "accepted answer" mechanic.

**Only the discussion author and repository maintainers** can mark an answer.

### To mark an answer (as the discussion author)

1. Navigate to the reply you want to mark as the answer
2. Look for the **"Mark as answer"** button below the reply
3. Activate it - the reply is pinned to the top and the discussion shows a green "Answered" badge

**Why it matters:** Marked answers make Q&A discussions into searchable documentation. Anyone who searches for the same question later immediately sees the correct answer without reading the whole thread.

**To unmark an answer:** Activate "Unmark as answer" on the same reply.

## 7. Polls

Some discussion categories support embedded polls. A poll lets you gather structured vote data from the community.

### Creating a poll

1. When creating a discussion, look for the "Add a poll" option below the body editor
2. Type each poll option (up to 8 options)
3. Set poll duration (optional)
4. Submit the discussion - the poll appears inline

### Voting in a poll

```text
Navigate to the poll section
→ Radio buttons or checkboxes for each option
→ Space/Enter to vote
→ "Vote" button → Enter
```

**Poll results:** After voting, percentages appear next to each option. Screen readers announce the count and percentage per option.

## 8. Screen Reader Navigation Reference

### Discussions List

```text
T                     → Navigate tab bar to reach "Discussions" tab
H / 2                 → Category section headings
3                     → Individual discussion titles (h3 links)
K                     → Navigate all links (discussions, categories, pagination)
Enter                 → Open a discussion
/                     → Focus the search bar (if supported)
```

### Inside a Discussion

```text
H                     → Original post heading and top-level reply headings
3                     → Individual replies
↓                     → Read body content
Tab                   → Move to interactive elements (reply buttons, reactions, mark as answer)
Ctrl+Enter            → Submit a reply (when in text area)
```

#### NVDA note

- Browse mode (NVDA+Space) to read the discussion
- Enter application mode for the reply editor
- Discussion replies are `<article>` elements - NVDA announces "article" as you navigate with H

#### JAWS note

- `A` key navigates `<article>` elements - useful for jumping between replies
- Use Forms Mode for the reply editor

#### VoiceOver note

- VO+Right to read through content
- VO+Command+L to list all links (useful for navigating many replies quickly)
- VO+Space on the reply field to enter interaction mode

## 9. Organization-Level Discussions

Some organizations enable Discussions at the organization level, separate from any repository. These work identically to repository discussions but span the whole organization.

Common uses:

- Org-wide announcements
- Community introductions ("Introduce yourself" pinned thread)
- Cross-repo feature brainstorming
- Community spotlights and events

Find them at `github.com/ORGANIZATION/discussions`.

## 10. Accessibility Agents: What's Different Here

Accessibility Agents prompts currently operate on **issues, PRs, and code** - not directly on Discussions. If you want to respond to a discussion using Accessibility Agents:

1. Copy the discussion URL or content
2. Use `/issue-reply` with the content pasted in: the agent will draft a thoughtful, accessible response
3. Paste the result back into the discussion reply editor

This works well for first-response drafts on Q&A threads or community questions in your area of expertise.

## GitHub Gists

>
> **Listen to Episode 23:** [GitHub Gists](https://lp.csedesigns.com/ggg/PODCASTS.html) - a conversational audio overview of this chapter. Listen before reading to preview the concepts, or after to reinforce what you learned.

## Shareable Code Snippets and Notes

> Gists are a simple way to share code snippets, notes, or small files without creating a full repository. Think of them as lightweight, version-controlled pastebins.

### Learning Cards: GitHub Gists

<details>
<summary>Screen reader users</summary>

- On the Gist creation page at gist.github.com, press `D` to jump to the main landmark, then `F` to navigate form fields: Description, Filename, Content, and Visibility buttons
- Your Gists page lists each gist as an `H2` heading with its description -- press `2` or `H` to jump between gists
- Gists are full Git repositories -- you can clone them with `git clone` and edit locally using your usual screen reader workflow in VS Code

</details>

<details>
<summary>Low vision users</summary>

- Gist pages use syntax highlighting matching GitHub's current theme -- switch between light and dark mode for comfortable reading
- Public and secret gists look identical on the page; the only difference is the URL visibility -- check the "Create secret gist" or "Create public gist" button label before submitting
- The revision history link appears at the top of any gist -- click "Revisions" to see a diff view of every edit

</details>

<details>
<summary>Sighted users</summary>

- Gists live at gist.github.com, separate from regular repositories -- each gist shows a syntax-highlighted code block with filename tabs at the top
- The visibility selector is a split button at the bottom of the editor -- the dropdown arrow reveals "Create secret gist" vs "Create public gist"
- You can add multiple files to one gist using the "Add file" button below the first editor pane

</details>

## What Is a Gist?

A Gist is a Git repository that holds a single file or a small collection of files. Every Gist:

- Has its own URL (e.g., `gist.github.com/username/a1b2c3d4`)
- Is version-controlled (you can see edit history)
- Can be **public** (anyone can see) or **secret** (only people with the link can see)
- Supports Markdown rendering
- Can be embedded in web pages
- Can be cloned, forked, and starred just like repos

**Secret does not mean private.** Anyone with the URL can view a secret Gist. It's just not listed publicly on your profile.

## When to Use a Gist vs a Repository

| Use a Gist When... | Use a Repository When... |
| --------------------  | --------------------------  |
| Sharing a single code snippet | Building a full project |
| Posting configuration examples | Collaborating with multiple people |
| Quick notes or documentation | Need issues, PRs, or project management |
| Sharing logs or error messages | Want CI/CD and automated checks |
| Small utility scripts | Need multiple branches |

## Creating a Gist

### Via GitHub Web Interface

1. Navigate to [gist.github.com](https://gist.github.com)
2. **Gist description:** A short title (e.g., "NVDA configuration for GitHub")
3. **Filename:** Name your file with extension (e.g., `nvda-config.txt`, `script.py`, `notes.md`)
4. **Content:** Paste or type your code/text
5. **Visibility:**
   - Select **"Create public gist"** for openly shareable content
   - Select **"Create secret gist"** for link-only sharing
6. The Gist is created with a unique URL you can share

#### Screen reader navigation

- `D` to cycle landmarks to "Main"
- `F` to navigate form fields
- Tab through: Description → Filename → Content textbox → Visibility buttons

### Adding Multiple Files to a Gist

You can add multiple files to a single Gist:

1. After typing the first filename and content, select **"Add file"** (button below the editor)
2. Repeat for each additional file
3. Create the Gist

**Use case:** Share related config files together (e.g., `.vscode/settings.json` + `.vscode/keybindings.json`)

### Learning Cards: Creating a Gist

**Screen reader users:**

- On the Gist creation page at gist.github.com, press `D` to jump to the main landmark, then `F` to navigate form fields in order: Description, Filename, Content textarea, and visibility buttons
- The visibility selector is a split button -- the main button creates a public gist; Tab to the dropdown arrow next to it and press Enter to reveal the "Create secret gist" option
- Each filename field has a corresponding content textarea directly below it -- after filling one file, Tab to the "Add file" button to add another file to the same gist

**Low-vision users:**

- The Gist editor uses the same syntax highlighting as regular GitHub files -- your current theme applies; increase font size in browser zoom for comfortable editing
- The split button for public vs. secret visibility is at the bottom of the form -- the two options look nearly identical; read the button label carefully ("Create public gist" vs. "Create secret gist") before clicking
- The "Add file" button appears below the first file editor as a small text link -- zoom in to find it; each additional file gets its own filename field and content textarea

**Sighted users:**

- The Gist creation form has three main fields stacked vertically: description at the top, then filename, then a large code editor -- fill all three before choosing visibility
- The visibility split button at the bottom-right has a dropdown arrow -- click the arrow to choose between public and secret; the default (larger) button creates a public gist
- Add multiple files to a single gist using the "Add file" link below the editor -- multi-file gists are useful for sharing related configurations or code snippets together

## Editing a Gist

1. Navigate to your Gist's URL
2. Select **"Edit"** (button in the top-right)
3. Make your changes
4. Select **"Update public gist"** or **"Update secret gist"**

Every edit creates a new revision. Click **"Revisions"** to see the full edit history.

## Embedding a Gist

You can embed Gists in web pages, blog posts, or documentation:

```html
<script src="https://gist.github.com/username/gist-id.js"></script>
```

GitHub renders it as a formatted code block with syntax highlighting and a link back to the Gist.

**Accessibility note:** Embedded Gists are `<iframe>` elements. Screen readers will announce them as "frame" and allow navigation into the content.

## Cloning a Gist

Every Gist is a Git repository. You can clone it:

```bash
git clone https://gist.github.com/username/gist-id.git
```

Make changes locally, commit, and push just like a normal repo.

## Forking a Gist

You can fork someone else's Gist to create your own copy:

1. View the Gist
2. Select **"Fork"** in the top-right
3. GitHub creates a new Gist under your account

**Use case:** Someone shares a useful script, you fork it, and customize it for your needs.

## Finding Your Gists

**Your Gists page:** [gist.github.com/your-username](https://gist.github.com/)

All your public and secret Gists are listed here. You can:

- Search your Gists by filename or content
- Star Gists you want to reference later
- Delete old Gists

### Screen reader navigation

- Each Gist appears as a heading (H2) with its description
- Press `2` or `H` to jump between Gists
- Each Gist has links: "Edit," "Delete," "Star," "Embed"

## Discovering Public Gists

**Browse trending Gists:** [gist.github.com/discover](https://gist.github.com/discover)

See popular Gists by language. Great for finding:

- Useful scripts and utilities
- Configuration examples
- Code snippets for learning

## Gist Comments

Public Gists support comments. Anyone with a GitHub account can leave a comment, making Gists useful for:

- Asking questions about a snippet
- Suggesting improvements
- Discussing implementation details

### To add a comment

1. Scroll to the bottom of the Gist page
2. `F` to navigate form fields → Find the comment textarea
3. Type your comment (Markdown supported)
4. `Ctrl+Enter` or activate "Comment" button

## Security and Privacy

### Public Gists

- Appear on your profile
- Are indexed by search engines
- Anyone can view, fork, and comment

### Secret Gists

- Do not appear on your profile
- Are not indexed by search engines
- Anyone with the URL can view
- Still version-controlled and can be starred

### Never put sensitive data in Gists

- Passwords or API keys
- Personal identifying information
- Proprietary code you don't have permission to share

If you accidentally post sensitive data:

1. Delete the Gist immediately
2. Revoke/regenerate any exposed credentials
3. Remember: Forks and clones may still exist

## Example Use Cases

### 1. Sharing Screen Reader Config

```text
Filename: nvda-github-config.txt
Content:
# NVDA Settings for GitHub Web Navigation
- Browse Mode: Use screen layout (enabled)
- Verbosity: Most punctuation
- Rate: 65%
- Keyboard shortcuts: Use standard GitHub shortcuts (G+I, G+P, etc.)
```

Share the Gist URL with other screen reader users.

### 2. Quick Markdown Note

```text
Filename: workshop-notes.md
Content:
# Workshop Day 1 Notes
- GitHub Flow: branch → commit → PR → review → merge
- Keyboard shortcuts: G+I (issues), G+P (PRs), / (search)
- Always link PRs to issues with "Closes #N"
```

Reference it later or share with workshop participants.

### 3. Code Snippet for a StackOverflow Answer

When answering questions, paste your code as a Gist and link to it. Readers get syntax highlighting, version history, and the ability to fork your solution.

## Gists vs GitHub Repositories - Quick Comparison

| Feature | Gist | Repository |
| ---------  | ------  | ------------  |
| Issues | No | Yes |
| Pull Requests | No | Yes |
| GitHub Actions | No | Yes |
| Projects | No | Yes |
| Multiple branches | No | Yes |
| Revisions/history | Yes | Yes |
| Forkable | Yes | Yes |
| Embeddable | Yes | No |
| Comments | Yes | Yes (on issues/PRs) |

## Deleting a Gist

1. Navigate to the Gist
2. Select **"Edit"**
3. Select **"Delete"** (top-right, after Edit button)
4. Confirm deletion
